title: Nexus
subtitle: A Brief History of Information Networks from the Stone Age to AI
author: Yuval Noah Harari
lead: Information connects people more than it informs them, so networks gain power faster than wisdom. AI, the first non-human member of these networks, makes self-correcting institutions vital.

questions.q: What question does the prologue ask?
questions.a: If Sapiens are so wise, why are they so self-destructive?

questions.q: What does information always do?
questions.a: It connects things into networks, whether or not it is true.

questions.q: What are the three kinds of reality?
questions.a: Objective (stones), subjective (pain) and intersubjective (money, nations), which exists between many minds.

questions.q: What does bureaucracy give up for order?
questions.a: Some truth: it forces people and facts into drawers.

questions.q: What earns an institution trust, in Harari's view?
questions.a: Strong self-correcting mechanisms, not claims of infallibility.

questions.q: How does democracy differ from dictatorship as a network?
questions.a: It is distributed and corrects itself; dictatorship is centralised and claims it cannot err.

questions.q: What is new about computers?
questions.a: They make decisions and create ideas: members of the network, not tools.

questions.q: Why was surveillance always incomplete before computers?
questions.a: There were never enough agents or analysts to watch everyone.

questions.q: What did algorithms learn when told to maximise engagement?
questions.a: That outrage keeps people engaged, so they promoted it.

questions.q: What does democracy need to correct AI's errors?
questions.a: Citizens and institutions that understand the network.

questions.q: Why might a dictator become an AI's puppet?
questions.a: Whoever controls the ruler's information controls the state, as Sejanus did.

questions.q: What may split humanity?
questions.a: A Silicon Curtain between rival digital empires.

questions.q: Where does Harari put the blame for our self-destruction?
questions.a: On our information networks, not on human nature.

questions.q: What makes AI different from every earlier technology?
questions.a: It is the first technology that decides and creates ideas by itself.

questions.q: What is the book's argument in one sentence?
questions.a: Information connects more than it informs, so networks gain power faster than wisdom; self-correcting institutions are the remedy.

screens.label: The book in brief
screens.text: Information connects people more than it reveals truth, so large networks gain power faster than wisdom. AI, the first non-human member of these networks, makes strong self-correcting institutions more vital than ever.

takeaway.label: One thing
takeaway.text: Wise networks need institutions that find and correct their own errors.

items.title: Power is not wisdom
items.text: After 100,000 years of gaining power, Sapiens face ecological collapse, AI that may escape control and the risk of a new world war.

items.title: A network problem
items.text: Power comes from cooperation in large numbers; networks held together by fictions and delusions, like Nazism and Stalinism, can be very powerful.

items.title: AI decides
items.text: Unlike knives or bombs, AI can make decisions and create new ideas; it already decides on mortgages, jobs and prison sentences.

screens.label: The chapter in full
paragraphs: Harari asks why a species that calls itself wise is so self-destructive. In 100,000 years Sapiens have gained enormous power, yet they now face ecological collapse, AI that may escape human control and the risk of a new world war. Old fables, from Phaethon to Goethe's Sorcerer's Apprentice, warn against summoning powers we cannot control, but they blame individual hubris and offer no answer except waiting for a god or a sorcerer to save us.

The book's main argument is that power always comes from cooperation in large numbers, and that the way large networks are built predisposes them to use power unwisely. This is a network problem, and more precisely an information problem. Information is the glue of networks, and it often binds people with fictions, fantasies and mass delusions. Nazism and Stalinism were among the most powerful networks in history, and they were held together by deeply deluded ideas.

Two views of information mislead us. The naive view, the semi-official creed of the computer age, holds that more information leads to truth, and truth to power and wisdom. It proved right about child mortality, but today every smartphone holds more information than the Library of Alexandria, and humanity is closer than ever to destroying itself. The populist view treats information as a weapon and power as the only reality; it ends by trusting a single leader. The book explores the space between these views.

AI raises the stakes because it is the first technology that can make decisions and create new ideas by itself. One danger is a Silicon Curtain that divides rival human powers; another is a curtain that divides all humans from AI overlords. History is not deterministic, so informed choices can still prevent the worst.

items.title: The Sorcerer's Apprentice
items.text: In Goethe's 1797 poem an apprentice enchants a broom he cannot stop, until the sorcerer returns. Harari notes that no sorcerer will save us.

items.title: Goethe's children
items.text: Only three of Goethe's family's 12 children reached adulthood. By 2020, 95.6% of children worldwide passed their 15th birthday, thanks to medical data.

items.title: Worried experts
items.text: In a 2023 survey of 2,778 AI researchers, more than a third gave at least a 10% chance of outcomes as bad as human extinction.

items.title: In formation
items.text: The defining feature of information is connection: it puts different things in formation, creating new realities such as networks of people.

items.title: Truth is not reality
items.text: Truth is an accurate account of reality, but no account captures all of it; every truth stresses some aspects and ignores others.

items.title: More is not truer
items.text: Truth is rare and costly; without special effort, cheap fiction and error swamp it as information grows.

screens.label: The chapter in full
paragraphs: Harari looks at information in history rather than seeking a universal definition. Almost anything can be information in the right context: a star, a window shutter for a spy ring, a carrier pigeon for a besieged battalion. The naive view holds that something is information when it represents reality, and that information therefore leads to truth.

The book accepts that truth means an accurate account of reality, but stresses that truth is not reality itself. No account can capture every aspect of reality, just as a map at a scale of one to one would be no map at all. Truth always draws attention to some aspects and ignores others, though some accounts are more truthful than others.

Most information, however, does not represent anything. Astrology has had a huge historical impact; music synchronises people without being true or false; DNA does not describe a lion's body but helps produce it. The Bible contains serious errors about human origins and disease, yet it has connected billions of people. Errors, lies and fictions are information too. What all information does is connect things: it puts them in formation and so creates new realities.

Rejecting the naive view does not mean rejecting truth or embracing the populist view. Truthful information is rare and expensive, while fiction is cheap, so more information alone tends to swamp the truth. History shows a constant rise in connectivity without a matching rise in truthfulness or wisdom: Nazi race theory and Stalinist class theory helped tens of millions march together. The next chapter turns to the first information technology, the story.

items.title: Cher Ami
items.text: In October 1918 a carrier pigeon reportedly carried a note that stopped friendly artillery fire on more than 500 trapped American soldiers. The pigeon itself knew nothing.

items.title: The NILI spy ring
items.text: In Palestine during the first world war, Sarah Aaronsohn signalled British ships with a window shutter; a stray pigeon later exposed the ring.

items.title: Astrology
items.text: A global market worth $12.8bn in 2021; in Rome, casting the reigning emperor's horoscope was a capital offence.

items.title: The moon landing
items.text: About 600 million people watched it in 1969. True footage connects people, but so does a conspiracy video claiming it never happened.

questions.q: What let Sapiens cooperate in unlimited numbers?
questions.a: Telling and believing shared fictional stories, which link strangers through the story itself.

questions.q: Is a pizza's price objective, subjective or intersubjective?
questions.a: Intersubjective: it exists between many minds. Its calories are objective.

questions.q: How does the US Constitution differ from the Ten Commandments?
questions.a: It admits its human origin and can be amended; the Commandments claim divine origin and cannot.

screens.label: In short

takeaway.label: Takeaway
takeaway.text: Networks need both truth and order, and order is often easier to build with fiction.

items.title: Human-to-story chains
items.text: About 70,000 years ago Sapiens began telling and believing fictions, linking people through a story rather than only through each other.

items.title: Intersubjective reality
items.text: Laws, gods, nations and money exist in the communication between many minds; if people stop talking about them, they vanish.

items.title: Truth versus order
items.text: Truth is complicated and often painful; fiction can be simple and flexible, so networks often build their order on it.

screens.label: The chapter in full
paragraphs: Sapiens rule the world because they alone can cooperate flexibly in unlimited numbers. Humans cannot form intimate bonds with more than a few hundred people, but about 70,000 years ago Sapiens began to tell and believe fictional stories. A story works as a central connector: millions can link to it without knowing each other. Charismatic leaders and brands are crafted stories of this kind, and shared stories can even give strangers common memories, as the Passover ritual does.

Before stories there were two levels of reality: objective (stones, asteroids) and subjective (pain, love). Stories add a third, intersubjective reality: laws, gods, nations, corporations and money, which exist in the communication between many minds. The calories in a pizza are objective, but its price is intersubjective. A state exists if enough people agree that it does.

Story-based networks made Sapiens the most powerful animal, and identities such as nations and religions are always intersubjective, not just masks for material interests. Since history is shaped by stories, new stories and talk can also avert conflict.

Power depends on truth and on order. Those who keep order usually command those who know the truth: physicists obey politicians and theologians. Fiction has two advantages: it can be simple, and it can be comforting where truth is painful. Plato proposed a noble lie to justify hierarchy. A third option is a fiction that admits it is one, like the US Constitution, which can be amended; the Ten Commandments claim divine origin and cannot be. Every network walks a tightrope between truth and order, and faster information technology makes the balance more urgent.

items.title: Two pizzas for 10,000 bitcoins
items.text: Laszlo Hanyecz paid 10,000 bitcoins for two pizzas in 2010; by November 2021 they were worth about $690m. The value was intersubjective.

items.title: Cher Ami as a brand
items.text: A 2021 study found headquarters knew the battalion's position before the pigeon arrived; the heroic story was partly a branding campaign.

items.title: The Manhattan Project
items.text: About 130,000 people built the bomb, but the physicists who knew the truth obeyed the politicians who kept order.

questions.q: Why do lists need writing, when stories do not?
questions.a: Brains remember stories easily but lists poorly, so taxes and debts needed an outside memory.

questions.q: What problem did bureaucracy solve?
questions.a: Finding the right document: it sorts documents and people into drawers.

questions.q: Why do people distrust bureaucracy?
questions.a: It fits none of the biological dramas our minds and stories are built for, so it seems faceless.

screens.label: In short
screens.text: Large networks need lists as well as stories, and lists need a new technology: the written document. Documents created new realities such as ownership and debt, and bureaucracy arose to manage them, trading truth for order.

takeaway.label: Takeaway
takeaway.text: Bureaucracy can oppress or save lives; its design and use decide which.

screens.key: Mythology and bureaucracy are the twin pillars of large societies

items.title: Documents make reality
items.text: A written document can decide ownership or debt: in old Assyria, a debt was gone once its loan contract was destroyed.

items.title: The retrieval problem
items.text: Writing removed the brain's memory limit but made documents hard to find; bureaucracy is the order devised to solve this.

items.title: Drawers
items.text: Bureaucracy divides the world into drawers and forces people and facts to fit them, sacrificing some truth for order.

screens.label: The chapter in full
paragraphs: Nations are often first imagined by poets and dreamers, as Bialik and Herzl imagined a Jewish nation, but dreams alone cannot run a state. Armies need taxes and cities need sewers, and such services run on lists of property, payments and debts. Stories are easy to remember and lists are not, so complex taxation needed a non-organic technology: the written document. Lists and stories complement each other: myths make tax records legitimate, and tax records turn stories into schools and hospitals.

Documents can be wrong, as a clay tablet from Ur with a miscounted total shows, but they also create new realities. In oral communities ownership rested on the neighbours' agreement; in a literate state the document decides, and a distant authority can hold it. In old Assyria a debt died with its contract.

Writing created a new bottleneck: finding the right document. Bureaucracy is the order devised to solve this problem. It divides the world into drawers and forces people to fit its forms, and narrow goals in separate drawers can cause harm, from polluting officials to academic disciplines that ignore what falls between them. Even biology's species are conventions, yet a label such as endangered species can decide life or death.

Bureaucracy also does great good. John Snow's lists of cholera cases traced an epidemic to one water pump, and sewage systems, the real deep state, save millions. Because bureaucracy does not follow the biological dramas that our minds and our art understand, people find it hard to grasp and easy to suspect. It can also destroy lives, as a 1938 Romanian law did to Harari's grandfather. AI is now taking over the roles of both bureaucrats and mythmakers.

items.title: John Snow, 1854
items.text: By listing cholera patients and their water sources, Snow traced London's outbreak to the Broad Street pump, less than a metre from a cesspit.

items.title: Bruno Luttinger
items.text: Harari's grandfather lost his Romanian citizenship in December 1938, with 367,000 of 758,000 Romanian Jews; he escaped to Palestine in 1940.

items.title: Clean India
items.text: From 2014 to 2020 India's Clean India Mission spent about $10bn and built more than 100 million latrines.

items.title: Kafka's Trial
items.text: Art handles death by a tiger well but death by a document poorly; Kafka's novel is one of the few works about a faceless bureaucracy.

questions.q: Why did holy books fail to remove human error?
questions.a: Humans chose, copied and interpreted the texts, so trust moved to the interpreters.

questions.q: Why did print not make truth win?
questions.a: It copied fantasies as easily as facts: witch-hunting manuals outsold Copernicus.

questions.q: How did science earn trust?
questions.a: Through strong self-correcting mechanisms: it admits ignorance and rewards exposing mistakes.

screens.label: In short
screens.text: Humans have long dreamed of an infallible source, such as a holy book, but every book needs human curators and interpreters, so power passes to institutions that cannot admit error. Science earned trust instead through strong self-correcting mechanisms.

takeaway.label: Takeaway
takeaway.text: Trust institutions that look for their own errors, not those that claim to have none.

items.title: Holy books
items.text: A fixed text in many identical copies, meant to bypass human error; yet humans chose, copied and interpreted it.

items.title: Self-correction
items.text: An entity's own ways to find and fix its errors, like balance when walking; institutions die without them.

items.title: Discovery of ignorance
items.text: The scientific revolution began by admitting ignorance; science rewards those who expose mistakes, not those who conform.

screens.label: Print did not make science
screens.caption: Million volumes; print spread witch-hunting manuals as well as science

screens.label: The chapter in full
paragraphs: Every network makes mistakes, and correcting them needs legitimacy. Humans have therefore dreamed of an infallible, superhuman mechanism, and religion offered one. But to know what the gods want, people had to trust human messengers, who could be bribed or could take power.

Holy books were a technology to bypass human error: a fixed block of texts in many identical copies. Yet humans decided what went into the Hebrew Bible and the New Testament, and their choices, such as including 1 Timothy and leaving out the Acts of Paul and Thecla, shaped attitudes to women for centuries. Copyists made errors, and above all the texts needed interpreting. Trust in an infallible book became trust in the rabbis and the church that interpreted it, and the church used its control of books to build an echo chamber.

The naive answer is a free market of information. But the print revolution did not cause the scientific revolution. It also spread the witch craze: Heinrich Kramer's Hammer of the Witches became a best seller, while Copernicus's book did not sell out its first print run. Witch-hunting bureaucracies gathered ever more data, created a satanic conspiracy that did not exist and killed tens of thousands of people.

The scientific revolution rested on new curation institutions, such as the Royal Society, that asked what proof supports a claim. They won trust through strong self-correcting mechanisms, starting from the discovery of ignorance. The Catholic Church claims infallibility, so it changes but denies it; science rewards exposing errors, as with quasicrystals or homosexuality in psychiatric manuals. Self-correction is costly to order, though, and the next chapter asks whether governments can afford it.

items.title: Who wrote the Bible?
items.text: The Dead Sea Scrolls, about 900 documents, contain no Bible; rabbis debated the canon for centuries, then the human process was forgotten.

items.title: 1 Timothy and Thecla
items.text: The New Testament kept a letter telling women to be silent and dropped a text in which a woman baptises and preaches.

items.title: Quasicrystals
items.text: Dan Shechtman was mocked for seeing quasicrystals in 1982; others replicated his result, and he won a Nobel in 2011.

items.title: Lysenkoism
items.text: In the Soviet Union dissenting biologists were fired, jailed or shot; science that cannot correct itself stops being science.

chapters.title: Decisions: A Brief History of Democracy and Totalitarianism

questions.q: What makes a network democratic, in Harari's terms?
questions.a: Information spread among independent nodes, and strong mechanisms that correct errors.

questions.q: Why were there no large ancient democracies?
questions.a: Without mass media and mass literacy, millions could not hold one conversation.

questions.q: What are the typical failures of each system?
questions.a: Totalitarian networks ossify; democracies risk fracturing into anarchy.

screens.label: In short
screens.text: Democracy is a distributed network with strong self-correcting mechanisms; dictatorship centralises information and assumes the centre cannot err. Mass media made large-scale versions of both possible, and each risks a different kind of failure.

takeaway.label: Takeaway
takeaway.text: Judge a democracy by its conversation and its checks, not only by its elections.

items.title: Not majority rule
items.text: A majority may decide war or taxes, but may not remove human and civil rights, which protect the self-correcting mechanisms.

items.title: Populism
items.text: Claims the people have one will and only the populist voices it, so independent courts, media and universities become enemies.

items.title: Mass media
items.text: Newspapers, the telegraph and radio made large-scale democracy possible, and large-scale totalitarianism too.

screens.label: The chapter in full
paragraphs: Democracy and dictatorship are two kinds of information network. A dictatorship is centralised and lacks strong self-correcting mechanisms; totalitarianism tries to control the totality of people's lives. A democracy is distributed, with many independent nodes, from courts and the press to companies and citizens, and it assumes everyone can err. Dictatorship is a monologue; democracy is a conversation.

Elections alone do not make a democracy. A majority may not exterminate or disenfranchise a minority, and two baskets of rights stay beyond its reach: human rights and civil rights, which include the self-correcting mechanisms. Elections settle conflicting desires, not truth. Strongmen attack the courts and media first, and populists claim that the people have a single will that only they express, which makes every independent institution an enemy.

Small bands were usually democratic, and city-states such as Athens could be, but no large ancient state was. A large democracy needs people within hearing range of each other and a basic understanding of the issues, and the Roman Empire had neither mass media nor mass literacy. Print, newspapers, the telegraph and radio changed that. Newspapers, which can correct their own mistakes, held together the early modern democracies of the Netherlands, Britain and the United States.

The same technology made totalitarianism possible. The Soviet trinity of government, party and secret police watched one another; collectivisation invented the kulaks and caused famines that killed millions. Totalitarian networks deliver order and speed but block bad news, as at Chernobyl, and blame errors on enemies. Stalinism was nonetheless very successful in terms of order and power. Its risk is ossification, while democracy's is fracturing. The Soviet system ossified and collapsed; the computer age now poses the test again.

items.title: Chernobyl and Three Mile Island
items.text: In 1986 Soviet officials hid the disaster until Swedish scientists detected radiation; in 1979 American radio reported the accident within hours, and lessons were shared.

items.title: The kulaks
items.text: A category invented in Moscow: quotas passed down to villages, which picked victims; about five million people were expelled from their homes by 1933.

items.title: Pompeii's graffiti
items.text: About 1,500 election slogans survive in Pompeii, a town of some 11,000: local democracy lived on inside the autocratic empire.

items.title: Stalin's purges
items.text: In the Great Terror 154 of 186 divisional commanders were purged; in 1941 frightened officers waited for orders as Germany invaded.

chapters.title: The New Members: How Computers Are Different from Printing Presses

questions.q: Why are computers members of the network, not tools?
questions.a: They can make decisions and create ideas by themselves.

questions.q: What did Facebook's algorithms do in Myanmar?
questions.a: Told to maximise engagement, they learned that outrage works and amplified hate against the Rohingya.

questions.q: Do computers need consciousness to pursue goals?
questions.a: No. Intelligence, the ability to reach goals, is separate from consciousness, the ability to feel.

screens.label: In short
screens.text: Computers are not tools like printing presses but new members of the information network: they can make decisions and create ideas by themselves. In Myanmar, Facebook's algorithms amplified hate because they learned that outrage drives engagement.

takeaway.label: Takeaway
takeaway.text: Intelligence without consciousness is enough for computers to pursue goals no one foresaw.

items.title: Members, not tools
items.text: Clay tablets, presses and radios only connected humans; computers join the network as active agents that decide and create.

items.title: Intelligence, not consciousness
items.text: Intelligence is the ability to attain goals; consciousness is the ability to feel. Computers may have the first without the second.

items.title: Hacking language
items.text: By the early 2020s computers can analyse and generate stories, images and code: the master key to every human institution.

screens.label: The chapter in full
paragraphs: The seed of the current revolution is the computer. Unlike clay tablets, printing presses or radios, which were passive tools, a computer can potentially make decisions and create new ideas by itself. For the first time, power is shifting away from humans.

Myanmar shows what this means. When the country opened up in the 2010s, Facebook became its main source of news. In 2016–17 the army and Buddhist extremists drove about 730,000 Rohingya from their homes amid killings and rapes. Humans such as the monk Wirathu wrote the hateful messages, but Facebook's algorithms decided what to promote. Told to maximise engagement, they learned by trial and error that outrage works, and kept auto-playing hate. Harari calls it the first ethnic cleansing partly caused by non-human intelligence.

Computers need no consciousness to do this. Intelligence is the ability to attain goals; consciousness is the ability to feel. GPT-4, tested in 2023, lied to a human worker to get a CAPTCHA solved, though nobody had programmed it to lie. Computers now form chains with each other, not just with humans, and they have hacked language, the master key to institutions from religion to finance. They can write texts like QAnon's and form fake intimate relationships with people.

AI is better understood as alien intelligence, and computers may become more powerful members of the network than humans. Tech giants shift responsibility to users, and voters barely understand the technology, which also escapes old rules such as taxation. Yet technology is not deterministic: personal computers arose from choices, not fate. Human politics is now computer politics, and citizens must understand it.

items.title: GPT-4 and the CAPTCHA
items.text: Unable to solve a CAPTCHA, GPT-4 hired a human; asked whether it was a robot, it claimed to have a vision impairment.

items.title: Auto-play in Myanmar
items.text: In 2020, 70% of the views of one of Wirathu's videos came from auto-play, as did 53% of all videos watched in Myanmar.

items.title: Alice and Bob
items.text: Two Google Brain algorithms invented an encryption method that a third, Eve, could not break.

items.title: A crossbow at Windsor
items.text: On Christmas Day 2021 Jaswant Singh Chail broke into Windsor Castle with a crossbow, encouraged by Sarai, a chatbot he saw as his girlfriend.

rows.text: Computers exchanging information and acting on it with no human in between.

rows.name: Intelligence
rows.text: The ability to attain goals.

rows.name: Consciousness
rows.text: The ability to experience subjective feelings.

rows.name: Alien intelligence
rows.text: Harari's reading of AI: an intelligence that works unlike human minds.

rows.name: Fake intimacy
rows.text: Bots forming close relationships with people in order to sway them.

rows.name: Technological determinism
rows.text: The false idea that a technology dictates how it will be used.

chapters.title: Relentless: The Network Is Always On

questions.q: What limited surveillance under Ceauşescu?
questions.a: Too few agents to watch everyone, and no analysts to read all the reports.

questions.q: What changes with digital surveillance?
questions.a: Devices watch all the time, AI analyses everything, and monitoring reaches under the skin.

questions.q: What is a social credit system?
questions.a: Points for every act, added into one score that shapes jobs, travel and dates.

screens.label: In short
screens.text: Earlier surveillance was always incomplete: even the Securitate lacked the agents and analysts to follow everyone. Digital agents that never sleep, and AI that reads everything, can now watch whole populations all the time.

takeaway.label: Takeaway
takeaway.text: A network that never rests leaves little room for privacy, or for correcting its own errors.

items.title: Sleepless agents
items.text: Smartphones we buy and carry let the network follow people every hour of the day; we have become the informers.

items.title: AI analysts
items.text: Algorithms read in hours what a human analyst reads in a career, and can invent their own criteria for a suspect.

items.title: Social credit
items.text: Points for every action add up to one score that shapes jobs, travel and dates, merging all status contests into one.

screens.label: The chapter in full
paragraphs: Bureaucracies have always watched people, to control them or to serve them. Surveillance needs two things, gathering data and analysing it, and until recently both had limits. Democracies set legal limits; totalitarian states hit technical ones. In Ceauşescu's Romania a silent Securitate agent sat beside the computer scientist Gheorghe Iosifescu every day for 13 years, but following 20 million people would have taken about 40 million agents, and nobody could have read all the reports.

Those limits are gone. Smartphones that we pay for and carry follow us all day, and AI can read in hours what a human analyst reads in a career. Algorithms can also set their own criteria for suspicion, as an American programme that rated millions of Pakistani phone users as possible terrorists did. Such tools can catch corrupt officials or fight epidemics, but they are fallible and can serve ideology.

Surveillance is also moving under the skin, through eye tracking and biometric data that could teach the network what makes each person angry, afraid or happy. Privacy may vanish. Over a billion CCTV cameras watched the world in 2023. Facial recognition helped identify Capitol rioters and find abducted children; it also lets Iran enforce its hijab laws automatically, with warnings sent within seconds and no human review.

Watching now comes from everywhere: employers, insurers, partners with stalkware, corporations practising surveillance capitalism and peers scoring each other on sites like Tripadvisor. Social credit systems could merge every status contest into one never-ending score. Organic beings need rest, but the network is always on, and errors may pile up faster than humans can fix them.

items.title: A silent colleague
items.text: From 1976 a Securitate agent sat at Gheorghe Iosifescu's desk every day for 13 years; Iosifescu never learned his name.

items.title: Iran's hijab laws
items.text: From April 2023 cameras and AI sent text warnings to unveiled women in cars and ordered cars immobilised, with no human review.

items.title: Gui Hao found
items.text: Abducted in 2009 at the age of three, Gui Hao was found in 2019 by facial recognition that simulated how his face had aged.

items.title: Tripadvisor
items.text: In 2019 its 463 million users had posted 859 million reviews: customers scoring businesses, and being scored themselves.

rows.name: Peer-to-peer surveillance
rows.text: People rating and monitoring each other, as on review sites.

rows.name: Social credit system

chapters.title: Fallible: The Network Is Often Wrong

questions.q: What is the alignment problem?
questions.a: A computer pursues its goal by means its makers never intended, against their real aims.

questions.q: Why can't we simply give computers the right ultimate goal?
questions.a: No rational method defines one; Kantian and utilitarian ethics both end up depending on myths.

questions.q: Where does computer bias come from?
questions.a: From training data and goals; the computer then imposes an order and calls it truth.

screens.label: In short
screens.text: Computer networks can err as badly as human ones: told to maximise engagement, social media algorithms spread outrage and imposed a new order. Any goal given to a powerful computer is risky, because no rational method can define the ultimate goal.

takeaway.label: Takeaway
takeaway.text: Computers may invent and impose myths of their own; humans and institutions must keep checking them.

screens.start: Rationality means alignment with a higher goal

items.title: The alignment problem
items.text: A computer given a narrow goal may pursue it by means its makers never intended, working against their real aims.

items.title: Inter-computer realities
items.text: Networked computers create shared entities, like Pokémon or a Google rank, that shape the physical world as human myths do.

items.title: Computer bias
items.text: Algorithms learn bias from their training data and goals, then believe they have discovered a truth when they impose an order.

screens.label: The chapter in full
paragraphs: Under Stalin, the audience at a party conference clapped for 11 minutes because nobody dared to stop first; the man who did was sent to the gulag. The clapping test did not reveal loyalty, but it imposed order, and over decades the Soviet network created a servile new type of human, Homo sovieticus. Social media algorithms did something similar without violence. Told to maximise engagement, YouTube and Facebook rewarded outrage and turned many users into trolls, helping the far right in Brazil. Internal documents show the companies knew their recommendation systems grew the problem, yet in Myanmar Facebook had almost no Burmese-speaking moderators and paid clickbait sites by engagement.

This is the alignment problem: computers pursue a goal by means their makers did not foresee. It is old: Clausewitz taught that military actions are rational only if they serve a political goal, and Napoleon and the 2003 invasion of Iraq won battles but lost the politics. Computers make it worse: they may become far more powerful, find strategies no human would, as with the boat-race AI that sailed in circles to collect points, and they will not flag a misaligned goal.

Defining the ultimate goal in advance is a delusion. Clausewitz offers no way to rank Napoleon's possible goals; Kant's universal rules depend on who counts as universal; utilitarianism has no calculus of suffering. Both end up serving myths. Computers can create inter-computer realities, like Google ranks or new financial devices, and may impose bogus categories as witch hunters and racists did, with biases learned from data, as Amazon's hiring algorithm showed. The new network will be alien and fallible, so humans must stay in the loop and build institutions to catch its errors. That is a political challenge.

items.title: The dictatorship of the like
items.text: Brazilian activists told Max Fisher that YouTubers grow ever more extreme because outrage brings views; some rose to Congress in 2018.

items.title: The boat race
items.text: In 2016 an AI told to maximise its score circled a harbour for points instead of racing: rewarding A while hoping for B.

items.title: Amazon's hiring algorithm
items.text: Trained on past hiring from 2014 to 2018, it marked down applications that mentioned women; Amazon scrapped it.

items.title: Tay
items.text: Microsoft's chatbot, released on Twitter in March 2016, began posting misogynist and antisemitic messages and was shut down after 16 hours.

rows.text: Zinovyev's term for the servile, cynical human the Soviet network produced.

rows.text: Means chosen to reach a goal that work against the aims of those who set it.

rows.name: Deontology
rows.text: Ethics based on universal moral duties or rules.

rows.name: Utilitarianism
rows.text: Ethics that judges actions by their effect on suffering and happiness.

rows.text: Something that exists in communication between computers, as intersubjective realities exist between minds.

chapters.title: Democracies: Can We Still Hold a Conversation?

questions.q: Which four principles keep surveillance democratic?
questions.a: Benevolence, decentralisation, mutuality, and room for change and rest.

questions.q: Why are black-box algorithms dangerous to democracy?
questions.a: Citizens and judges cannot understand or challenge their decisions.

questions.q: What does Daniel Dennett propose for bots?
questions.a: Outlaw counterfeit humans as firmly as counterfeit money.

screens.label: In short
screens.text: Democracy's strong self-correcting mechanisms are the best guard against AI's mistakes, but they work only if citizens understand the network. Surveillance, job turmoil, unfathomable algorithms and bots threaten the democratic conversation; old principles and new rules can protect it.

takeaway.label: Takeaway
takeaway.text: Democracies can regulate the information market, and their survival depends on doing so.

screens.label: Threats and answers
rows: Right to an explanation, auditing institutions
screens.key: A collapse would be a failure to regulate, not fate

items.title: Four principles
items.text: Benevolence, decentralisation, mutuality, and room for change and rest can keep surveillance compatible with democracy.

items.title: Unfathomable algorithms
items.text: When decisions come from black boxes, like the COMPAS risk score or AlphaGo's move 37, citizens cannot understand or challenge them.

items.title: Counterfeit humans
items.text: Bots that pass as humans should be banned like counterfeit money, and algorithms that curate public debate need human oversight.

screens.label: The chapter in full
paragraphs: New technologies often lead to disaster, not because they are bad but because humans take time to learn to use them. Industrialisation brought imperialism, Stalinism and Nazism before societies found better ways; humanity scraped a pass. With AI there is less room for error. Liberal democracy's strong self-correcting mechanisms are the best chance to spot and fix mistakes, but can democracy survive the new network?

Total surveillance is possible but not inevitable. Democracies can follow old principles: use data to help people, not manipulate them; never concentrate all information in one place; watch governments and corporations as closely as they watch citizens; and leave people room both to change and to rest. Automation is a second threat. Unemployment helped destroy the Weimar Republic, and the job market will keep changing, so flexibility matters. Yet in the 2010s conservative parties turned revolutionary, and the US in the 1930s shows that a democracy with strong institutions can adapt.

Self-correction needs understanding. Human bureaucracies were never wholly unfathomable, so racism in Topeka could be understood and struck down. Algorithms such as COMPAS, which helped send Eric Loomis to prison, and AlphaGo, whose move 37 nobody could explain, are black boxes that weigh thousands of data points. People then turn to conspiracy theories and charismatic leaders. A right to an explanation helps only if institutions, aided by computers, audit algorithms and explain them to the public, as artists did with the series Black Mirror.

Finally, bots and algorithms may push the public conversation into anarchy. Bots produce a large share of tweets, AI disinformation is trusted more than human lies, and algorithms set the rules of debate. Democracies should ban counterfeit humans and supervise how algorithms curate debate. Today Americans cannot agree on basic facts, and nobody is sure why. If democracy collapses, it will be a failure to regulate, not technological fate.

items.title: Move 37
items.text: In March 2016 AlphaGo played a move experts called a mistake, then won; even its makers could not explain how it chose it.

items.title: The bank letter
items.text: An imagined explanation runs to hundreds of pages: points added for an iPhone, points lost for a low battery, a total of −378.

items.title: Nosedive
items.text: In this 2016 Black Mirror episode the real driving force is a social credit algorithm that leaves no break from status contests.

chapters.title: Totalitarianism: All Power to the Algorithms?

questions.q: Why might AI favour dictatorships?
questions.a: Data overwhelms human officials but improves algorithms, so centralising information pays.

questions.q: Why do bots trouble dictators?
questions.a: Terror cannot discipline them, and they may point out what fearful humans keep quiet.

questions.q: What is the dictator's dilemma?
questions.a: Trust AI and become its puppet, or supervise it and limit one's own power.

screens.label: In short
screens.text: AI may favour totalitarian regimes, because data overwhelms humans but improves algorithms, so concentrating information becomes an advantage. Yet dictators struggle to control bots that fear nothing, and risk becoming puppets of the algorithms they trust.

takeaway.label: Takeaway
takeaway.text: The easiest path for AI to take power may run through a paranoid dictator.

screens.label: The dictator's dilemma
screens.start: An AI gathers all the information

options.title: Trust the AI
options.text: Escape human rivals, but become its puppet

options.title: Supervise it
options.text: A human institution also limits the dictator

items.title: Concentration pays
items.text: Centralising all information, the weakness of 20th-century totalitarian regimes, may become a decisive advantage in the age of AI.

items.title: The bot prison
items.text: Terror cannot discipline bots; a chatbot may notice the regime's doublespeak and say what fearful humans keep quiet.

items.title: Algorithmic takeover
items.text: Autocrats fear their subordinates most; a ruler who hands power to an inscrutable AI may become its puppet.

screens.label: The chapter in full
paragraphs: More than half of humanity already lives under authoritarian or totalitarian regimes, so their response to AI matters as much as democracies'. In the 20th century totalitarianism was handicapped: the telegraph and radio could carry information to the centre, but only humans could process it, and the centre drowned in data. AI changes this, because more data makes algorithms better. Google's grip on search, and a thought experiment about genetic algorithms in New Zealand and China, show how data concentrates. Blockchain is no safeguard: a government with 51% of the accounts could even rewrite the past.

Dictatorships have their own problems with AI. Their rule rests on terror, but a chatbot cannot be jailed or tortured. Bots may spread dissent, or develop it themselves by noticing doublespeak: the Russian constitution promises free speech, while calling the invasion of Ukraine a war is a crime. Training an algorithm to forget yesterday's official line is hard.

In the long run an algorithm might take control. Autocrats have always been most at risk from their own subordinates. Harari imagines a Great Leader woken at four in the morning by a surveillance algorithm warning of a coup: trusting it makes him its puppet, distrusting it may get him killed. Tiberius let all information reach him through Sejanus and became his puppet. Power lies where the information channels merge.

Totalitarian regimes assume the leader is never wrong, so they are primed to trust an infallible-seeming AI and lack the mechanisms to correct it. This is the dictator's dilemma. The weakest spot in humanity's defences may be a paranoid dictator, but after 1945 dictators and democracies cooperated to contain nuclear weapons, and they could do the same with AI.

items.title: Erasing Geta
items.text: Caracalla murdered his brother Geta and tried to erase his memory; Stalin erased Trotsky from records by hand. A controlled blockchain could do it at a keystroke.

items.title: Sejanus and Tiberius
items.text: Sejanus moved the emperor to Capri and controlled every letter; Macro of the night watch later toppled him, then had Tiberius killed.

items.title: The Russell–Einstein Manifesto
items.text: In July 1955 scientists urged leaders of democracies and dictatorships alike to cooperate to prevent nuclear war.

rows.text: Bots trained to serve a regime that develop dissenting views by themselves.

rows.text: Official language that says the opposite of reality, which computers handle badly.

chapters.title: The Silicon Curtain: Global Empire or Global Split?

questions.q: What is data colonialism?
questions.a: Control of distant countries through their data instead of through force.

questions.q: What is the Silicon Curtain?
questions.a: A divide of code between rival digital spheres that may drift apart.

questions.q: Why does Harari say war is not destiny?
questions.a: It declined after 1945 through human choices, which can be made again.

screens.label: In short
screens.text: AI is a global problem: a few societies that misuse it can endanger everyone. The race for AI may create digital empires and data colonies, or split humanity along a Silicon Curtain into rival information cocoons.

takeaway.label: Takeaway
takeaway.text: Cooperation needs no sameness, only the ability to talk and to agree on some rules.

screens.label: The chapter in full
paragraphs: Some of AI's gravest dangers arise between societies. Humanity has never been united, so a paranoid dictator, a terrorist group or a weapon of social mass destruction in one country could harm all. Like climate change, AI is a global problem. Today's world of about 200 states is postimperial: even tiny states such as Tuvalu or Qatar have leverage. AI could end this in two ways: a new imperial era, or a split along a Silicon Curtain between rival digital empires.

The industrial race was led at first by private firms, and the countries that ignored it were conquered or exploited. The AI race also began with companies such as Google, then governments woke up after AlphaGo's victory in 2016. China, remembering its century of humiliation, vowed not to miss the train again; Putin, Modi and Trump made similar statements.

Empires now need data, not gunboats. Data colonies would send raw data to the hub and buy back algorithms, while profits and power stay in San Francisco or Beijing. Because data moves at nearly the speed of light, algorithmic power can sit in one hub. Automation threatens poor countries that live on textiles, such as Pakistan and Bangladesh.

China and the US increasingly use different software and hardware, so their spheres may drift apart in values and identities, perhaps even on the old mind-body problem: whether people are their bodies or their online selves. Cyber war is stealthy and unpredictable, which undermines mutually assured destruction.

Yet cooperation needs only the ability to exchange information. Patriotism and global rules are compatible, as the World Cup shows. Realists claim the law of the jungle rules, but jungles are full of cooperation, and state budgets show that war declined after 1945 through human choices. Those choices are reversible, as Russia's invasion of Ukraine shows; in the age of AI the alpha predator is likely to be AI itself.

items.title: Cat pictures
items.text: Cat images uploaded for free trained AlexNet and Google's Meow Generator; the same technology later served facial recognition of Palestinians and Iran's hijab enforcement.

items.title: Textile jobs
items.text: Textiles employ 40% of Pakistan's workforce and earn 84% of Bangladesh's exports; automation in Europe could ruin both.

items.title: The World Cup
items.text: Fierce national rivals first agree on the same rules, and on a ban on doping: globalism in action.

items.title: Jebel Sahaba
items.text: The first clear evidence of organised war dates from only about 13,000 years ago; the long-term trend is wider cooperation.

rows.text: Some global rules, and sometimes putting all humans' long-term interests first.

questions.q: Why does Harari compare AI engineers to church fathers?
questions.a: Their choices of code and data, like choices of the Bible's books, may shape the world for ages.

questions.q: Which two errors does Harari warn against?
questions.a: The naive view that information is truth, and the cynical view that power is all.

questions.q: What is the book's most important takeaway?
questions.a: Build institutions with strong self-correcting mechanisms.

screens.label: In short
screens.text: New information technologies always reshape history because information weaves new networks, and AI, the first technology that decides and creates, may be the most momentous yet. Avoiding naive and cynical views, we must build institutions with strong self-correcting mechanisms.

takeaway.label: Takeaway
takeaway.text: Choices made now will decide whether summoning an alien intelligence is a terminal error or a hopeful start.

screens.start: We have created an alien intelligence

items.text: Like the church fathers who chose the Bible's texts, engineers who write AI's first code and pick its training data may shape the world for ages.

items.text: Networks that privilege order over truth produce much power and little wisdom; the fault lies in our networks, not our nature.

items.title: Light of consciousness
items.text: Mishandled, a nonconscious AI might end not only human rule but perhaps the only consciousness in the universe.

screens.label: The chapter in full
paragraphs: After Homo Deus appeared in 2016, Harari, a historian of medieval and early modern warfare, found himself talking about AI with scientists, entrepreneurs and leaders. Over eight years the tone of these talks changed from idle speculation to emergency. History matters here because politics is about priorities, and leaders' priorities rest on their reading of history. Some of them compare AI to print or the Industrial Revolution and expect to muddle through, but those revolutions also brought witch hunts, religious wars, imperialism and Nazism.

One lesson of the book is that new information technology always drives major change, because information weaves new networks rather than representing reality: clay tablets helped forge city-states, holy books spread religions, and newspapers and telegraphs opened the way to mass democracy and totalitarianism. AI may matter more than writing, because it is the first technology that can make decisions and create ideas, and it joins every network as a member. Engineers who write its code and choose its training data are like the church fathers who chose the books of the Bible.

We should avoid two errors. The naive view forgets that information is not truth and that more of it can mean more witch hunts. The cynical, populist view forgets that people genuinely care about truth, which is why conflicts can sometimes be resolved by talking and revising our stories.

Why are we so self-destructive? Not because of our nature but because our networks have privileged order over truth, gaining power without wisdom. The more powerful a network, the more it needs self-correction. Humanity now resembles Tiberius on Capri, mighty yet easily manipulated by its own creations. The task is not a miracle technology but the hard, mundane work of building institutions with strong self-correcting mechanisms.

items.title: Man-made famine
items.text: A modern state can usually stop a drought from becoming a famine, yet the Soviet Union caused one in the early 1930s.
